topic: database theory; functional dependencies; incomplete information; vague and disjunctive tables
status: bounded theory lead from one sampled Fundamenta Informaticae 2018 full text; no novelty claim
claim: For the paper's chosen FD desiderata, the model representation changes what is possible: P-functional dependencies satisfy the full list on vague tables, whereas no FD semantics can satisfy that same list on the more expressive disjunctive-table model; weak-FD seamless satisfaction is NP-complete. This is a conditional model/axiom boundary, not a universal impossibility for every definition of incomplete data or every notion of desirable FD semantics.
positive_evidence: The paper states and motivates a cross-model set of properties, including Armstrong-style axioms, independence from irrelevant attributes, and seamless satisfaction.
Theorem 6.1/6.4 proves an impossibility for the complete listed package on disjunctive tables and constructs PFDs satisfying it on vague tables.
Proposition 7.1 proves checking seamless satisfaction for weak FDs is NP-complete; PFD checking is supported by an index over possible left-side valuations.
counterevidence: The properties are selected and justified intuitively by the authors, not derived as a uniquely accepted community standard.
The result compares two specific incomplete-information models; other probabilistic, null, or symbolic representations may have different semantics and complexity.
The paper itself calls for investigating other and maximal sets of desiderata and more expressive models; no later full taxonomy was established in this targeted search.
falsifiable_test: Specify a formal lattice of incomplete-table representations and candidate FD desiderata, then prove membership, implication, and decision complexity for each model/property pair. The lead narrows if a published semantics already meets the same axioms on a representation at least as expressive as disjunctive tables; it strengthens if further impossibility/tractability boundaries are proved. This batch did not construct the taxonomy or prove new results.
limitations: One theory paper, one chosen desiderata set, no expert/user study on semantic acceptability, and only targeted follow-up search. The question is a research-design lead, not empirical prevalence or novelty evidence.

topic: database cleaning; functional dependencies; optimal subset repair; optimal update repair; most-probable database
status: bounded complexity-status finding from one sampled PODS 2018/TODS 2020 full text plus adjacent 2024 primary-source check
claim: Complexity claims for FD-based repair must name the operation. The sampled paper establishes a polynomial/APX-complete dichotomy for optimal subset repairs and thereby resolves the general-FD most-probable-database dichotomy, but optimal cell-update repairs are a distinct problem: some FD sets have easy subset repair and APX-complete update repair, while other sets reverse that relation. A full update-repair dichotomy remains open in the expanded TODS paper. Later soft-FD classification is adjacent and does not settle this hard-update gap.
positive_evidence: Theorem 3.4 gives a dichotomy for optimal S-repairs: polynomial-time when the FD-set test succeeds and APX-complete otherwise, including unweighted duplicate-free inputs.
Theorem 3.10 reduces the general-FD most-probable-database open case to the S-repair dichotomy and resolves it.
Section 4 gives sufficient conditions, APX-hard cases, and examples where S- and U-repair complexity reverse; it explicitly states that a full dichotomy for optimal U-repairs remains open.
The 2024 soft-FD TODS paper studies a different objective and gives algorithms for special cases including one FD and bipartite matching; its general classification is still partial.
counterevidence: This is a bounded complexity-theory literature status, not evidence that practical data cleaning systems fail or that all update-repair instances are hard.
The full U-repair problem has constant-factor approximation guarantees under stated conditions; the open dichotomy is not absence of useful algorithms.
The 2024 soft-constraint problem is related but distinct and must not be misrepresented as a direct resolution of hard U-repair complexity.

sources.title: Database Repairing with Soft Functional Dependencies
sources.sections: Official ACM abstract and scope; general soft classification remains partial

falsifiable_test: Develop a necessary-and-sufficient structural criterion over FD sets for polynomial-time exact U-repair, with matching hardness on the complement; separately classify restrictions on replacement values and weighted inputs. Any candidate dichotomy is falsified by one FD set on the wrong side or one reduction invalidating its hardness claim. No theorem was reproved or extended in this audit.
limitations: The sampled proof was reviewed but not independently re-proved. The soft-FD follow-up was checked at abstract/publication scope, not audited as a complete proof. This does not assert practical impact or novelty.

topic: spatial databases; graph databases; spatial co-location mining; clique enumeration
status: bounded systems-evaluation lead from one sampled arXiv 2018 full text and targeted 2024 publisher abstract check
claim: A materialized neighborhood graph and clique traversal can reduce repeated spatial-neighbor work for the sampled Chicago-crime co-location task, but the measured evidence is tied to one 30,000-incident, 33-category dataset and the fastest of three proposed algorithms trades memory for speed. At 20,000 vertices, increasing the threshold 0.4→0.5 km takes 111.4 seconds incrementally versus 313.8 seconds for graph creation (about 2.8×, not orders of magnitude); at 30,000 vertices/0.3 km, the slowest proposed method takes 12,837 seconds. A 2024 graph-based method is related but not a controlled replication.
positive_evidence: The paper models co-location as clique enumeration over a Titan neighborhood graph backed by Cassandra, with MongoDB and Elastic components; its thread pool is 48 workers.

On up to 30,000 graph vertices, CliqueExtend is consistently faster than CliqueEnumG/K in the reported tables; at N=30,000 and R=0.3 km reported times are 392.4, 578.5, and 12,837.2 seconds, respectively.
For N=20,000 and a 0.4→0.5 km threshold update, graph update takes 111.4 seconds vs 313.8 seconds for a fresh graph construction, supporting a bounded reuse benefit.
counterevidence: The “large real-world” data is 30,000 incidents and 33 crime types from one city; no cross-city/general-domain replication was reported in the sampled paper.
The update saves a factor of about 2.8 in the cited case, not orders of magnitude, and still takes over 100 seconds; calling all query/update workflows interactive is regime-dependent.
CliqueExtend uses extra storage; its fastest run is not a free improvement, and one threshold's runtimes cannot establish a universal advantage over relational spatial joins or modern graph engines.
The 2024 publisher-hosted GSCM paper uses a different adaptive-neighborhood/logical-reasoning method and does not supply a controlled reproduction of the Titan algorithms.

sources.version: v1 / arXiv preprint; venue not verified
sources.sections: Section VI experimental setup and Tables V–IX; conclusion

sources.title: Graph-based spatial co-location pattern mining: integrate geospatial analysis and logical reasoning

falsifiable_test: On identical geospatial snapshots and neighborhood definitions, compare spatial joins, graph traversal, and modern spatial/graph engines while varying event count, feature skew, threshold, memory, and threshold-update frequency. Charge ingestion/materialization, full rebuild, incremental update, query runtime, and peak storage; verify exact pattern equality. The lead weakens if graph traversal fails to improve total build-plus-query cost or if incremental updates lose their advantage under larger or changing data. No systems experiment was run.
limitations: One older preprint system on one city sample plus an abstract-level later comparator; exact reproducibility/artifacts were not audited. The result is a testable benchmark lead, not a broad scalability claim.
